en: Score = 50 + 10 × (√(1 − luck share) × skill + √(luck share) × luck), with skill and luck standard normal. This gives both trials the same spread and a correlation of 1 − luck share, so the regression slope equals the reliability (when the true effect is 0). The theory value is (luck share) × how far above 50 the top group averaged in trial 1, taken from the tail mean φ(z)/cut share of the normal distribution.

You can verify with node tools/validate-regression.js. The numbers above average 400 repeats of a 400-person sample, and the same seed gives the same result. Graph ④ averages 3 runs of 40 samples each.
The code is available on GitHub.
Survivorship Bias: Bullet Holes on Returning Planes · Simulatio Lab
Returning planes have the most holes in the wings and fuselage. Should the armor go there? Run survivorship bias yourself.
Bullet Holes on the Planes That Came Back: Where Should the Armor Go?

Looking at the planes that came back from battle, the wings and fuselage carry the most bullet holes. So it seems obvious that armor belongs where planes get hit most. But all we ever see are the planes that came back. A plane hit in the engine did not return, so engine holes are almost invisible to us. Should the armor go where the holes are, or where they are missing?

The plane drawing is split into five sections: engine, cockpit, fuselage, wings and tail. Each bullet lands on a random point of the plane, so larger sections (wings, fuselage) get hit more. A plane takes 3 hits per sortie on average.
Each section has a different chance that one bullet brings the plane down. The engine (slider) and cockpit (40%) are deadly; the fuselage, wings and tail are around 5% or less.

Only planes that did not go down come back to be inspected. The left picture shows only the holes on returned planes; the right shows every bullet that actually hit (red dots belong to planes that never came back).

A bullet hitting an armored section is stopped with 70% probability. You can armor only as many sections as the budget slider allows, and the same bullets and the same luck are used to compare with and without armor.

The story comes from work attributed to Abraham Wald of Columbia University's Statistical Research Group in the Second World War. The widely told version is heavily simplified, though, and this model is a simplified one built by this project to understand the story, not a reproduction of the actual report.

What it shows: Averaged over 200 seeds, the default setting (engine lethality 50%, 2,000 sorties, 2 sections armored) gave a survival rate of 67.9% without armor. Armoring the fuselage and wings, where returned planes have the most holes, raised it only 3.4 points to 71.3%, while armoring the engine and cockpit, where holes are missing, raised it 15.4 points to 83.3% (the exact values are 68.0%, 71.4% and 83.3%). In all 200 runs the intuitive choice was fuselage and wings and the Wald-style choice was engine and cockpit. The reason is in graph ②: the share of bullets that you can still see on returned planes was 33.8% for the engine and 40.5% for the cockpit, but 64.5 to 65.8% for the fuselage, wings and tail. The deadlier a section, the more of its evidence disappears, so "few holes" should be read not as "rarely hit" but as "if hit, it does not come home". The result depends on the sortie count and the engine lethality. Raising the engine lethality from 0% to 90% never let the intuitive choice win (missing-hole armor 90.5% vs hole-based armor 87.6% at 0%, 79.4% vs 60.6% at 90%, averaged over 100 seeds), because the cockpit stays deadly. With a budget of 1 section it was 78.3% (missing holes) vs 69.7% (hole-based), and with 3 sections 85.2% vs 72.7%. With only 100 sorties the Wald-style choice found the best pair in 85% of 200 seeds, and from 500 sorties on, in 100%.

What it doesn't show: This is not the content of Wald's actual report. The popular story is boiled down to one line, "armor the places without holes", but Wald's work was about mathematically estimating the chance of surviving a hit in each section from returned planes only, and the specific sections and numbers differ between retellings. Here the section areas, lethalities and the armor effect (70%) are all chosen by this project, and the model simply assumes that each bullet lands independently at a single point. Real bullets pass through several sections and vary with the aircraft, the mission and the enemy weapons. The model knows the lethalities, which in reality are unknown, so the Wald-style choice is imitated by a simple rule, "pick the sections with the fewest holes", and it can go wrong with few sorties. It also does not mean that "armor where planes are hit most" is always wrong: if every bullet were equally deadly, the holes on returned planes would look like the real hits. The same logic may apply to any situation where we learn only from successes, but this page runs only the one aircraft model.
